b: PDD Holdings, the group behind the Pinduoduo and Temu shopping platforms, cut its sales and marketing expenses to RMB25.3 billion in the third quarter of 2026 from RMB30.3 billion a year earlier, while total revenues stood still at RMB108.3 billion (US$16.2 billion). Inside that unchanged top line, revenues from online marketing services and others rose 12% to RMB59.8 billion and transaction services revenues fell 12% to RMB48.5 billion, according to unaudited results for the three months ended September 30, 2026, which the Dublin and Shanghai-based company released on November 19, 2026, and furnished to the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission on Form 6-K.

PDD Holdings, which owns Temu and Pinduoduo, brought in almost exactly the same revenue between July and September as a year before, but spent about RMB5 billion less on sales and marketing, and its operating profit rose by roughly a quarter. For brands and sellers, the striking change is inside the revenue: money from online marketing services grew 12% and now outweighs transaction services, which fell 12%, and the company has not explained why. PDD says it is moving spending toward logistics, overseas warehousing and merchant support, and its finance head told analysts that a single quarter's expense ratios should not be read as a trend.

All figures come from PDD Holdings' earnings release, published as Exhibit 99.1 to the Form 6-K, unless marked with an asterisk as a PPC Land calculation. Percentage changes without an asterisk are the company's own. PPC Land's calculations use the release's figures in millions of renminbi. The release converts at RMB6.7045 to US$1.00, the Federal Reserve H.10 noon buying rate for September 30, 2026.

One figure in the release is wrong. The highlights section states total revenues as "RMB108.3 billion (US$116.2 billion)." The detailed results section gives US$16.2 billion, and the income statement gives US$16,159 million, which matches the stated exchange rate. The same kind of slip appeared in JD.com's release two days earlier, where PPC Land found net revenues printed as US$146.2 billion in the highlights of JD.com's third quarter results.

A year ago, transaction services was the larger of PDD's two revenue lines, at RMB54.9 billion against RMB53.3 billion for online marketing services and others. The positions have now reversed. Online marketing services brought in RMB59.8 billion (US$8.9 billion) in the quarter, RMB11.3 billion more than transaction services, according to PPC Land's calculation.

The two moves almost cancel out. Online marketing services added RMB6.47 billion year on year, while transaction services lost RMB6.41 billion, leaving total revenues RMB64 million higher than in the third quarter of 2025. That is how a 12% rise and a 12% fall produce a flat quarter.

What makes the third quarter unusual is how sharply it breaks from the first half of the year. Subtracting the third quarter from the nine-month totals in the release gives the first-half figures below.

For the first nine months of 2026, the release puts total revenues at RMB326.9 billion, up 6.2% by PPC Land's calculation from RMB307.9 billion. Online marketing services rose 6.1% over the nine months to RMB167.4 billion and transaction services 6.2% to RMB159.5 billion, both PPC Land calculations. In other words, transaction services grew more than five times as fast as online marketing in the first half, then went into reverse.

Neither the release nor the call explains the swing. The release names the two lines "online marketing services and others" and "transaction services" without defining them, and it does not say how much of either comes from Pinduoduo in China or Temu abroad. It does not report gross merchandise volume (GMV), buyer numbers or order counts, so the share of sales PDD keeps as revenue, its take rate, cannot be derived from the documents. On the call, Jun Liu, the company's VP of Finance, read out the two revenue figures and moved on to costs.

For advertisers, the online marketing line is the closest PDD comes to disclosing a retail media network: money merchants spend to be seen by shoppers inside a marketplace. At RMB59.8 billion, it was 2.1 times the RMB28.1 billion JD.com reported for marketplace and marketing revenues in the same quarter, according to PPC Land's calculation, though JD.com's line also carries commissions and the two companies define their lines differently.
Spending less on sales and marketing

The release attributes the 12% fall in total operating expenses, to RMB31.9 billion, "primarily" to lower sales and marketing expenses. That line dropped by RMB5.0 billion. On a non-GAAP basis, according to Liu, sales and marketing expenses were RMB24.9 billion against RMB29.8 billion, or 23% of revenues against 28% a year earlier. Total non-GAAP operating expenses fell to 28% of revenues from 32%.

The cut is concentrated in the third quarter. Over nine months, sales and marketing expenses were RMB88.7 billion, down 2.4% from RMB90.9 billion, which implies a first half of RMB63.4 billion, up 4.7% on the first half of 2025, by PPC Land's calculation. PDD spent more on sales and marketing than a year earlier in the first six months, then spent markedly less in the next three.

The release does not break the line down. It does not say how much went on media bought from search engines, social networks or other platforms, how much on promotions and subsidies, and how much on staff. Share-based compensation inside sales and marketing fell to RMB370 million from RMB526 million.

Joyce Ju of Bank of America put the question directly. Noting "solid expense ratio discipline this quarter," Ju asked: "Can investors expect these efficiency gains to continue? On the flip side, could lower spending pressure consumer mindshare and market share over the longer term?"

Liu's answer declined to treat the quarter as a template. "As previously communicated, the company's financial performance and expense ratios in any given quarter fluctuate with the pace of our business rollouts and their return cycles. Single-quarter metrics should not be extrapolated as a reliable indicator of future trends," Liu said. "We remain in the strategic investment phase of our 100 billion support program."

On the marketing question itself, Liu gave a position that will interest any platform that sells ads to e-commerce companies. "Regarding consumer monetary mindshare, we believe that a consumer's genuine appreciation comes from the price they pay and the services they receive with each purchase, rather than short-term marketing expenditure," Liu said. "Consistently building these fundamental e-commerce capabilities, such as supply chain capabilities, is the foundation of our long-term competitiveness."

The release carried a similar line from Liu: "We remain in a strategic investment phase, focused on strengthening supply chain capabilities and supporting our merchants. We will maintain investment discipline while funding initiatives that support a healthy merchant ecosystem and strengthen our platform's long-term competitiveness."
Where the money is going instead

Research and development is the one expense line that grew. It rose to RMB5.1 billion from RMB4.3 billion on a GAAP basis, an increase of 16.8% by PPC Land's calculation, and to RMB4.6 billion on a non-GAAP basis, up 24%, according to Liu. Over nine months, research and development spending reached RMB14.0 billion, up 22.1% from RMB11.5 billion.

The balance sheet points the same way. Property, equipment and software, net, rose to RMB6.4 billion at September 30, 2026, from RMB1.3 billion at December 31, 2025, nearly five times the earlier figure by PPC Land's calculation. The release does not say what was bought or where. Net cash used in investing activities rose to RMB37.8 billion in the quarter from RMB11.6 billion a year earlier, but that line also includes purchases of short-term investments and deposits, and the release gives no separate capital expenditure figure.

Management described the spending in terms of programs rather than amounts. Co-Chairman and Co-Chief Executive Officer Jiazhen Zhao said the company had extended its 100 billion support program "beyond platform operations to include more stages in the supply chain, such as R&D, production, and fulfillment," and that the third quarter "marked a full year toward our vision for a new decade of high-quality development." Zhao, and Chen during the questions, spoke in Chinese; the English renderings quoted in this article are the interpretation given on the call, which the company said is "for reference only." In the release, Zhao put it more briefly: "During the past quarter, we continued to deepen our support for the merchant ecosystem, helping merchants develop better products and reach new consumers. We see significant potential to build on this progress and will continue investing in the tools and services that help our merchants grow."

Zhao also pointed to the company's first-party brand model, under which PDD has "established partnerships with merchants across industrial belts at scale," as part of a "three-year strategic goal of building another PDD." Lei Chen, the other Co-Chairman and Co-Chief Executive Officer, gave the reasoning. "Our role as a platform is to bring our understanding of consumer trends into the R&D and production process, helping our industry partners translate their manufacturing strengths into more competitive products. This is also a key rationale behind developing first-party brand business," Chen said. During the quarter, according to Chen, the team "worked with them to produce and launch high-quality first-party products at scale." No sales figure, product count or category list was given for the first-party business.

A marketplace that defines, quality-checks and launches its own branded products sits in a different position from one that only sells visibility to independent merchants. How far PDD intends to take this is not stated in the documents.
Competition at home: "no platform is pulling back"

Alicia Yap of Citigroup opened the questions by noting that competition among e-commerce platforms in quick commerce had moderated over the past two quarters. "So at this juncture, how does management view the competitive landscape in the domestic e-commerce? Has it reached a new equilibrium? And how is company approaching the pace of investment going forward?"

Zhao did not describe an equilibrium. "From what we are seeing across the broader e-commerce market, competition in China's e-commerce remains intense. This is driven by inherent characteristics of the industry. Consumers compare prices, quality, and services all over again each time they shop online, and it is easy for them to switch from one platform to another. As a result, no platform is pulling back. We see everyone is building on their strength to improve their capabilities on all fronts," Zhao said.

On pace, Zhao said investment "will vary from project to project." A fulfillment service that has proved effective in some regions will be assessed for whether it can run "in more regions reliably and at a reasonable cost" before the company decides how quickly to scale it. "These investments may take a long time to deliver results," Zhao said, "but we will remain firmly committed to investing in the areas that create long-term value for our merchant ecosystem and also for the platform's capabilities."

Rural logistics was the example offered. In remote villages, according to Zhao, parcels often went only as far as nearby towns, "leaving consumers to travel more than 10 km in some cases to collect them." One passion fruit seller received "more than 20,000 orders for delivery to villages over the past six months," and in regions covered by the company's free shipping to villages program, "many merchants have seen order volumes grow by over 30%." The company gave no figure for the program's cost, the number of villages covered or the share of orders it represents. Zhao framed the logistics push as something the company, now entering "our 12th year," is better equipped to tackle than before.
How the merchant and IP programs work
Executives described five programs on the call in enough detail to record how each operates. The descriptions below are theirs; the company published no program terms alongside the results.

Free shipping to villages. Run with logistics partners, according to Zhao: "The platform covers the shipping cost from county level transit hubs to village pickup points, bringing parcels directly to villages." Zhao said order volumes for fresh produce, general merchandise, home appliances, agricultural supplies and farming equipment "surged significantly" in covered regions during the quarter.

2026 Duoduo Premium Produce Initiative. An upgraded version introduced this year to help agricultural merchants improve quality and standardization, with "more resource support for products with geographical indications." The tools named were "improving certification, establishing dedicated shopping channels, and providing targeted resources." In the third quarter it reached Meishan for citrus, Rong'an for kumquats, Wuming for Wogan mandarins, Dalian for aquatic products and Tonglu for osmanthus.

Duoduo Harvest Season. Launched in the third quarter, it brought together "300,000 agricultural merchants on our platform across more than 1,000 agricultural regions nationwide," according to Zhao, with dedicated shopping sections, platform subsidies and traffic support.

IP protection program with the International AntiCounterfeiting Coalition. According to Chen, the expanded cooperation gives participating brands "an escalation channel for reporting IP infringement, with every submission receiving a response within 48 hours." Brands "can also submit keywords and images to help us identify potentially infringing product listings before complaints are even filed."

Shared overseas warehousing. Chen said PDD is "replicating the full range of e-commerce warehouse operations across different markets," covering receiving, storage, sorting, packing, shipping and returns, and "offering them as supply chain services to SMEs worldwide." The stated aim is that "merchants can hold inventory closer to consumers without making large upfront capital investments."

Zhao gave case figures from three production regions. In Tonglu, Zhejiang Province, platform merchants paid a premium for local osmanthus, "allowing some farmers to increase their income by over CNY 10,000 in just five days." In Linyi, Shandong Province, outdoor-goods merchants that moved from contract manufacturing to their own brands saw "annual sales have grown more than tenfold" and now produce "over 90%" of core components in-house. In Gaoyang, Hebei, "over 60% of local textile companies have undergone digital transformation." None of these figures can be checked against the release.
Platform governance: 30 measures in a quarter

PDD introduced "more than 30 targeted governance measures" during the quarter and "over 180 governance measures" since the start of 2026, according to Zhao. Several of the areas named concern how products are described and promoted:
Governance area named on the call

The company did not publish the measures themselves, the dates they took effect or the number of listings or merchants affected. Zhao also said the company donated CNY 10 million to each of two regions in Tibet hit by landslides and an earthquake, and that the fifth Duoduo Smart Agriculture Competition attracted 46 teams and more than 300 participants.
The release and the call never mention Temu by name. The international operation appears only as "our global business," and Chen's description of it was the most cautious passage of the call.

"At the same time, our global business is facing new challenges. International trade rules and regulatory requirements across different markets continue to evolve. These trends are increasing operational uncertainties and place higher demands on our existing supply chain and service capabilities," Chen said. "We will further step up our investments in the supply chain and strengthen our platform ability to adapt to different markets."

In the release, Chen said: "As our global business adapts to an evolving trade and regulatory environment, we remain committed to deepening our supply chain investments. By helping merchants serve consumers with greater efficiency and reliability, we are building a more resilient platform that delivers long-term value for the local communities we serve."

Asked by Yap how trade and tax changes were affecting cross-border sellers, Chen said: "These changes are making it more complicated for merchants to plan their business, manage inventory, and arrange fulfillment. SME merchants are indeed facing considerable pressure and challenges." Chen added that because smartphone adoption and online payments are already widespread in the company's major markets, "the main focus is logistics, fulfillment, and supply chain capabilities."

No market was named. PPC Land's own record shows what those "trade rules and regulatory requirements" have looked like for Temu. Temu stopped all Google Shopping advertising in the United States on April 9, 2025, as tariffs on Chinese imports rose. The U.S. then ended duty-free entry for packages valued at US$800 or less, with effect from August 29, 2025 for shipments outside the postal network, closing the de minimis route that low-value parcels had used. In Europe, finance ministers agreed on November 13, 2025 to scrap the €150 customs duty exemption, and from July 1, 2026 the EU began charging €3 per item on parcels worth less than €150.

Regulators have been active on the platform side too. The European Commission fined Temu €200 million under the Digital Services Act on May 28, 2026 over its assessment of risks from illegal products, gave the company four months to implement an action plan in October, and on November 17, 2026, two days before the results, issued preliminary findings that could lead to a fine of up to 6% of turnover over Temu's checks on unsafe products. In the United States, Temu agreed to a Texas data settlement that can cost it US$8 million per failed audit. The IACC cooperation Chen described follows Temu's corporate membership of the International Trademark Association, announced in July 2025.
The release gives no revenue, profit or user figures for the international business, so the effect of any of these measures on the third quarter cannot be measured from the documents.

Operating profit rose 24.5% to RMB31.2 billion by PPC Land's calculation, and the operating margin widened to 28.8% from 23.1%. Very little of that reached the bottom line. Net income attributable to ordinary shareholders was RMB29.5 billion, up 0.7% from RMB29.3 billion.

Two lines absorbed the gain. Net interest and investment income fell to RMB5.4 billion from RMB8.6 billion, down 37.1%, even though cash and short-term investments grew. Income tax expenses rose to RMB6.6 billion from RMB4.0 billion, lifting the effective tax rate, measured against profit before income tax and share of results of equity investees, to 18.2% from 12.0% by PPC Land's calculation. The foreign exchange loss widened to RMB408 million from RMB266 million. The release does not explain the tax increase or the fall in investment income.

The nine-month figures contain a larger, unexplained item. "Other (loss)/income, net" was a loss of RMB9.5 billion for the nine months to September 30, 2026, against income of RMB3.3 billion a year earlier. The third quarter contributed only a RMB70 million loss, so roughly RMB9.4 billion of the nine-month loss fell in the first half, according to PPC Land's calculation. Nine-month net income was RMB69.3 billion, down 7.4% from RMB74.8 billion, while nine-month operating profit rose 17.3% to RMB78.5 billion.
Cash, cash equivalents and short-term investments

Other non-current assets "mainly included time deposits, held-to-maturity debt securities, and available-for-sale debt securities," according to the release. Accumulated other comprehensive income swung to a loss of RMB9.2 billion from a gain of RMB2.1 billion at the end of 2025. Net cash generated from operating activities was RMB43.0 billion in the quarter, against RMB45.7 billion a year earlier, and RMB85.1 billion over nine months, up 2.8% by PPC Land's calculation. The diluted weighted-average share count fell to 5,897 million from 5,954 million.

Investing.com, whose transcript page says its summary was "generated with the support of AI and reviewed by an editor," presented the results as an earnings beat and a revenue miss. By its numbers, non-GAAP diluted earnings per ADS of CNY 21.04 beat a consensus of CNY 18.93 by 11.15%, while revenue of CNY 108.3 billion missed a forecast of CNY 116.16 billion by 6.73%. The consensus figures are Investing.com's; neither appears in PDD's documents.

Investing.com reported that PDD shares rose 5.87% in premarket trading to US$82 from a previous close of US$77.45, below a 52-week high of US$125.36 and above a low of US$71.94. Two of its characterizations do not match the release. It said the non-GAAP operating margin "held at 30%," but the release's own figures give 25.0% for the third quarter of 2025, by PPC Land's calculation. It also gave a current ratio of 2.62, whereas the September 30 balance sheet works out at 2.69, by PPC Land's calculation of current assets over current liabilities.

PDD's sales and marketing line came to RMB25.3 billion, or US$3.8 billion, in a single quarter, even after the cut. When a buyer of that size spends RMB5.0 billion less than a year before, the platforms that sell e-commerce advertising feel it, even though the release does not say whose inventory lost out.

The pattern is not limited to PDD. Two days earlier, JD.com reported a 26% cut in marketing expenses for the same quarter, mostly from more efficient food delivery subsidies. In Europe, Smarter Ecommerce data showed that the share of advertisers meeting Temu in Google Shopping auctions had fallen by around half since March 2026, as the €3 parcel charge arrived. Pinterest blamed part of the slowdown in its European ad growth to 12% in the second quarter on Asia-based cross-border retailers hit by regulatory action, without naming them. Amazon, whose low-price Haul storefront was described by Bloomberg as aimed at Temu, said Haul's buyer count had grown nearly 350% year over year, without giving a base.

The other side of PDD's business matters just as much to brands that sell on its platforms. Online marketing services now accounts for more than half of PDD's revenue, 55.2% in the quarter against 49.3% a year earlier, by PPC Land's calculation. That rise came while the company spent less on its own promotion, cut operating expenses and reported no growth at all. Revenue from selling marketing services rose, in other words, in the same quarter that PDD spent less buying marketing for itself. Whether that reflects higher prices, more advertisers, a change in how fees are classified or a shift between Pinduoduo and Temu, the documents do not say.

Liu's remark that customer loyalty comes "from the price they pay and the services they receive with each purchase, rather than short-term marketing expenditure" came from a company that still spent US$3.8 billion on sales and marketing in three months. One quarter does not make a policy, as Liu was careful to say. The direction of this one, though, is plain: less money spent on promotion, more money earned from selling it.

The release does not mention Temu or Pinduoduo, splits revenue by neither platform nor geography, and reports no GMV, take rate, buyer, merchant or order figures. It gives no guidance, no breakdown of sales and marketing spending, no capital expenditure figure and no explanation for the 12% fall in transaction services, the higher tax charge or the RMB9.5 billion nine-month other loss. The first-party brand business, the governance measures and the merchant programs were described on the call without costs or results that can be checked against the filing.

Who: PDD Holdings Inc., the Nasdaq-listed owner of Pinduoduo and Temu, with Co-Chief Executive Officers Jiazhen Zhao and Lei Chen and VP of Finance Jun Liu; analysts Alicia Yap of Citigroup and Joyce Ju of Bank of America questioned management on the call.

What: Revenues were flat at RMB108.3 billion as online marketing services and others rose 12% to RMB59.8 billion and transaction services fell 12% to RMB48.5 billion. Sales and marketing expenses fell to RMB25.3 billion from RMB30.3 billion, operating profit rose to RMB31.2 billion, and net income edged up to RMB29.5 billion as lower investment income and a higher tax charge absorbed most of the operating gain.
When: The results cover the three months ended September 30, 2026, and were released and furnished on Form 6-K on November 19, 2026, with an earnings call at 7:30 AM ET the same day.

Where: PDD Holdings is headquartered in Dublin, Ireland, and issued the release from Dublin and Shanghai; its businesses serve consumers in China and, through Temu, in overseas markets the company did not name.

Why: The results show an e-commerce group that still spent US$3.8 billion on sales and marketing in the quarter spending markedly less on sales and marketing while earning more from the marketing services it sells to its own merchants. Management said the money is going into supply chain, logistics and merchant support, and that the quarter's spending ratios should not be read as a trend, a stance that matters to media owners that sell ads to cross-border retailers and to brands that buy visibility on PDD's platforms.
